source.title: On Peace of Mind
source.attribution: Seneca, On Peace of Mind (trans. Aubrey Stewart), Standard Ebooks, public domain
source.notes: Taken from Seneca, Dialogues (trans. Aubrey Stewart), Standard Ebooks. Original date approximate.

cards.title: Changing places won't help if you bring the problem with you
cards.body:
Seneca describes people who keep moving, from city to country, trip to trip, chasing relief from restlessness. It never works, because they pack themselves along. The trouble isn't in the place but in the person.

A new job, city or holiday can be good, but it won't fix a habit of discontent. If the same irritation follows you everywhere, the work is inward: noticing what you're actually running from and dealing with that directly.
cards.quote: what we suffer from is not the fault of the places but of ourselves
cards.apply_it: Think of a change you're craving. Ask: what feeling do I hope it will remove? Write one way to address that feeling where you are.

quiz.question: Why, according to Seneca, does constant travel fail to bring peace?
options: The fault lies in ourselves, not in places
quiz.explanation: We take ourselves along, so a change of scene cannot cure an inner problem.

cards.title: Size up yourself and the task before taking it on
cards.body:
Seneca advises a frank estimate of your strengths before you commit, because most of us think we can do more than we can. Then weigh the task: the bearer should be stronger than the load. Beware of jobs that keep spawning more work, and prefer things you can finish or walk away from.

That's sound advice for saying yes at work or volunteering. A project that quietly doubles in scope can crush someone who agreed in a burst of optimism.
cards.quote: It is above all things necessary to form a true estimate of oneself, because as a rule we think that we can do more than we are able … for the bearer ought always to be more powerful than his load
cards.apply_it: Before your next yes, write down how long it will really take and whether you could stop if it grows. Then decide.

quiz.question: What rule of thumb did Seneca give about taking on tasks?
options: Always take on more than you can handle
The bearer ought to be stronger than the load
quiz.explanation: Compare your strength to the task; loads too heavy for the bearer crush him.

cards.title: Add a quiet "unless something prevents it" to your plans
cards.body:
Seneca suggests planning with a reserve clause: I'll sail, unless something stops me; this deal will succeed, unless something goes wrong. The wise person isn't spared setbacks, but they're never blindsided, because they expected some resistance from the start.

It's not pessimism. You still commit fully. You just don't promise yourself the outcome, so a delay or a no stings less and you can adapt faster.
cards.quote: I will set sail unless anything happens to prevent me, I shall be praetor, if nothing hinders me, my financial operations will succeed, unless anything goes wrong with them.
cards.apply_it: For one plan today, say or write it with the clause: "…unless something prevents it." Notice how it changes your feelings about the outcome.

quiz.question: What is the point of Seneca's "unless something prevents me" clause?
options: To lessen the pain of disappointment by expecting possible obstacles
To give yourself an excuse to quit
quiz.explanation: Expecting resistance means setbacks hurt less when they come.

cards.title: Meet the world's follies with a laugh rather than tears
cards.body:
When human foolishness and wrongdoing get you down, Seneca suggests copying Democritus, who laughed, rather than Heraclitus, who wept. Taking a wider view lets you bear things more lightly.

He adds that the laugher actually has more hope: mocking a mistake assumes it can be fixed, while weeping gives up. When the news or office politics feel overwhelming, a little wry humour can keep you engaged without sinking into despair.
cards.quote: we should imitate Democritus rather than Heraclitus … We must take a higher view of all things, and bear with them more easily: it better becomes a man to scoff at life than to lament over it.
cards.apply_it: Next time the news or a situation gets you down, look for the absurd side of it and share a gentle laugh with someone.

quiz.question: Whose attitude did Seneca recommend imitating?
quiz.explanation: He preferred Democritus's laughter, which keeps hope that things can improve.

cards.title: Wearing a mask all the time is exhausting
cards.body:
Seneca warns that hiding your real self and living for appearances is a constant source of strain. You end up watching yourself, afraid of being caught out, and you can't relax if you assume everyone is weighing your worth.

Honest simplicity has its risks, as some people may look down on it, but Seneca thought those risks were lighter than permanent pretence. Being open doesn't mean oversharing; it means not living a curated performance.
cards.quote: life is neither happy nor safe when one always has to wear a mask
cards.apply_it: Notice one place today where you're performing rather than being honest. Try a small, genuine response there instead.

quiz.question: What did Seneca say about always wearing a mask?
options: Life is neither happy nor safe that way
quiz.explanation: Constant self-watching and fear of exposure make such a life neither happy nor safe.

cards.title: Thinking you've already arrived is what stops you growing
cards.body:
The dialogue opens with Seneca's friend Serenus confessing his inner struggles. One of his sharpest observations is that we are our own biggest flatterers. We look kindly on our own faults, skip over the uncomfortable parts and assume we're further along than we are.

Many people, he suggests, would have become wise if they hadn't believed they were wise already. Honest self-assessment, including asking others for feedback, keeps the door open to real progress.
cards.quote: I fancy that many men would have arrived at wisdom had they not believed themselves to have arrived there already
cards.apply_it: Ask someone you trust: 'What's one thing I could do better?' Listen without defending yourself.

quiz.question: What does Serenus say stopped many people from becoming wise?
quiz.explanation: Self-flattery convinces us we've arrived, so we stop trying to improve.

cards.title: Trust that you're on the right path, even if you still feel wobbly
cards.body:
Serenus feels neither sick nor well, swinging between ideals and old habits. Seneca compares him to someone recovering from a long illness who keeps checking for a fever that isn't there. Like a lake still rippling after the storm has passed, he is not unwell, just not used to being well.

Seneca's prescription is not harsh self-criticism but confidence: believe you're heading the right way and don't get distracted by every side track. Progress often feels uncertain before it feels solid.
cards.quote: have confidence in yourself, and believe that you are proceeding on the right path, without being led aside by the numerous divergent tracks of wanderers
cards.apply_it: List three positive changes you've made in the past year. Remind yourself of them next time you feel you're getting nowhere.

quiz.question: What remedy did Seneca recommend for Serenus's unsettled mind?
options: Punish himself sternly for every slip
Have confidence that he was on the right path
quiz.explanation: Serenus needed self-trust, not harsh self-reproach.

cards.title: Peace of mind means a steady course, not constant highs
cards.body:
Seneca borrows the Greek idea of euthymia and calls it peace of mind. He defines it as a mind that keeps a steady, unruffled course, is content with itself, enjoys its surroundings, and is neither carried away by joy nor dragged down by gloom.

This is a useful target in a world that sells constant excitement. Peace of mind isn't feeling great every moment; it's an even keel that lets you meet good and bad days without being thrown off balance.
cards.quote: What we are seeking, then, is how the mind may always pursue a steady, unruffled course, may be pleased with itself, and look with pleasure upon its surroundings
cards.apply_it: Rate your mood each evening this week from 1 to 10. Aim for steadiness rather than peaks, and notice what keeps you level.

quiz.question: How does Seneca describe peace of mind?
options: A steady, unruffled course, neither elated nor depressed
Never feeling any emotion at all
quiz.explanation: Peace of mind is an even, contented state that isn't swept up or knocked down.

cards.title: Idleness quietly breeds envy
cards.body:
Seneca explains how restless dissatisfaction grows. People with unfulfilled hopes who sink into idleness start watching others' progress with bitter jealousy. Unable to succeed themselves, they begin to wish everyone else would fail, complain about the times and brood in corners.

If you notice resentment towards others' success, it may be a sign that your own energy needs somewhere to go. Envy often shrinks when we're working on something meaningful of our own.
cards.quote: for an unhappy sloth favours the growth of envy, and men who cannot succeed themselves wish everyone else to be ruined.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel envious of someone's progress, use that feeling as a cue: spend 20 minutes on a goal of your own.

quiz.question: What does Seneca say unhappy idleness tends to produce?
quiz.explanation: Idle, frustrated people often resent others' progress and wish them to fail.

cards.title: You can serve your community without a title or office
cards.body:
Seneca quotes the philosopher Athenodorus: you don't need public office to be useful. Someone who encourages young people, teaches good values where good teachers are scarce, or holds back friends rushing after money and luxury is serving the public too, even from a private life.

This matters for anyone who feels shut out of formal power. Mentoring a younger colleague, guiding a neighbour's child or speaking sense to a friend are real contributions, often more lasting than official roles.
cards.quote: such a man does service to the public though in a private station.
cards.apply_it: Find one young person in your family, workplace or community you can encourage or teach something this month.

quiz.question: According to Athenodorus as quoted by Seneca, who serves the public?
options: Anyone who guides and teaches others well, even privately
quiz.explanation: Teaching and guiding others counts as public service even without an office.

cards.title: When one door closes, find another way to be useful
cards.body:
Seneca imagines someone blocked at every turn: can't join the army, so seek civic office; can't hold office, so be an advocate; silenced, so give quiet advice; even barred from public life, so be a good friend and a decent guest. There's always some way to contribute.

He adds that sometimes the barrier is our own pride, refusing any role but the top one. If your preferred path is closed, don't give up on being useful. Look for the next door, however humble.
cards.quote: Thus, it is never possible for so many outlets to be closed against your ambition that more will not remain open to it
cards.apply_it: Think of a path that's closed to you right now. List three other ways you could still contribute in that area.

quiz.question: What does Seneca suggest when one route to contributing is blocked?
options: Wait until the original route reopens
Insist on nothing less than the top role
Find another outlet; some will always remain open
quiz.explanation: So many outlets can never all be closed; there's always some way to be useful.

cards.title: Staying safe doesn't mean burying yourself
cards.body:
Seneca points to Socrates in Athens under the Thirty Tyrants, when the city's best citizens were being killed. Socrates still moved among the people, comforting the grieving, encouraging those who had lost hope, and showing what it looked like to live freely among oppressors.

Seneca's conclusion: adapt to circumstances, step back when you must, but don't freeze in fear. Even in hard times there is room to keep your integrity and to help others in whatever way remains open.
cards.quote: but in any case we ought to move and not to become frozen still by fear
cards.apply_it: Is fear keeping you from doing something good you could still safely do? Take one small step towards it this week.

quiz.question: What example does Seneca give of keeping virtue alive under oppression?
options: Socrates in Athens under the Thirty Tyrants
quiz.explanation: Socrates kept encouraging and comforting others even in a city ruled by tyrants.

cards.title: Avoid commitments that keep growing and won't let you go
cards.body:
Seneca warns against tasks that aren't big in themselves but lead to more and more business, pulling you into new obligations. He also advises against starting anything you can't withdraw from. Choose things you can finish, or at least hope to finish.

Today we call this scope creep. A 'small favour' that becomes a monthly role, a side project that swallows your weekends. Before agreeing, ask: can I finish this, and can I step back if I need to?
cards.quote: apply yourself to something which you can finish, or at any rate can hope to finish
cards.apply_it: Before saying yes to your next request, ask: 'When does this end, and how would I step back if needed?'

quiz.question: Which kind of task does Seneca warn against taking on?
options: Ones that keep growing and won't stop where you intended
quiz.explanation: Tasks that multiply into more business, and from which you can't retreat, should be refused.

cards.title: Choose work that suits your nature
cards.body:
Seneca says you must decide whether you're better suited to active work or to quiet study and reflection, and follow your natural bent. He tells how Socrates led one man away from public speaking, thinking he'd do more good writing history. Forcing your mind into work it hates, Seneca says, achieves nothing.

That doesn't mean avoiding all discomfort. But knowing your strengths and steering towards roles that fit them makes you more effective and less drained.
cards.quote: for no good is done by forcing one’s mind to engage in uncongenial work: it is vain to struggle against Nature.
cards.apply_it: List the tasks that energise you and those that drain you. Find one way to shift a bit more of your week towards the first list.

quiz.question: What does Seneca say about forcing your mind into uncongenial work?
options: It is the only way to succeed
No good is done; it's vain to struggle against nature
It makes you happier in the long run
quiz.explanation: Seneca advises following the bent of your nature rather than fighting it.

cards.title: A trusted friend is one of life's greatest blessings
cards.body:
Seneca says nothing delights the mind like faithful friendship. He describes the ideal: someone you can tell your secrets to safely, whose knowledge of your actions you fear less than your own conscience, whose conversation eases your worries and whose advice helps your plans, whose cheerfulness lifts your gloom, and whose very presence is a joy.

Such friends are rare and worth cultivating. They don't appear by accident; they grow through time, honesty and showing up for each other.
cards.quote: whose conversation removes your anxieties, whose advice assists your plans, whose cheerfulness dispels your gloom, whose very sight delights you!
cards.apply_it: Think of the friend who best fits Seneca's description. Tell them this week what they mean to you.

quiz.question: According to Seneca, what delights the mind more than anything?
quiz.explanation: Seneca praises faithful friendship as the greatest delight of the mind.

cards.title: Steer clear of people who complain about everything
cards.body:
Seneca warns that habits spread between friends, like illness in a plague. Choose friends who are as free as possible from strong cravings and vices. He accepts that perfect people are hard to find, so pick the least bad.

Above all, he says, avoid gloomy people who grumble about whatever happens. Even if they're loyal, someone who meets every event with a groan will slowly wear down your peace of mind. Chronic negativity is contagious.
cards.quote: Above all, however, avoid dismal men who grumble at whatever happens, and find something to complain of in everything.
cards.apply_it: Notice who leaves you drained after a conversation. Limit time with chronic complainers, or gently steer talk to something constructive.

quiz.question: Which kind of companion does Seneca say to avoid above all?
options: Gloomy people who grumble at everything
quiz.explanation: Even a loyal friend can destroy your peace if they groan at every event.

cards.title: Have enough to avoid poverty, but not so much that you fear losing it
cards.body:
Seneca calls property the richest source of human sorrow. Losing money hurts more than never having it, and the rich feel their losses just as sharply as the poor. The more you own, the more you're exposed to fortune's blows, like a soldier too big for his armour.

His practical target: enough to keep you out of poverty, but not far beyond it. Beyond a comfortable sufficiency, extra possessions often bring more worry than happiness. Decide what 'enough' means for you.
cards.quote: the best amount of property to have is that which is enough to keep us from poverty, and which yet is not far removed from it.
cards.apply_it: Write down what 'enough' means for you: monthly income, savings, possessions. Use it to guide your next spending decision.

quiz.question: What amount of property does Seneca recommend?
options: Enough to keep from poverty, but not far beyond it
Exactly as much as your neighbours
quiz.explanation: A modest sufficiency protects you without exposing you to great losses.

cards.title: Don't just keep living the way you happened to start
cards.body:
Among the kinds of restlessness Seneca describes, one is easy to miss: people who aren't fickle at all, but who owe their consistency to dullness rather than choice. They carry on, not living as they would wish, but as they happened to begin.

Sticking with something isn't always a virtue. Your job, habits or routines may simply be where inertia left you. It's worth asking now and then: if I were choosing today, would I choose this? If yes, good. If not, you can begin to change course.
cards.quote: who go on living not in the way they wish, but in the way they have begun to live.
cards.apply_it: Pick one routine you follow without thinking. Ask: 'Would I choose this today?' If not, change one small part of it.

quiz.question: What does Seneca say about some people who seem consistent?
options: They have carefully chosen their path
They are the happiest of all
They live as they began, not as they wish
They change their plans too often
quiz.explanation: Some people's consistency comes from inertia, not from a deliberate choice.

cards.title: Judge things by their use, not by how they look
cards.body:
Seneca says that without thrift no wealth is ever enough, and with it none is too little. He urges us to set aside showing off and measure things by what they do: food to satisfy hunger, drink to quench thirst, clothes to serve their purpose. Get your riches from yourself, not from fortune.

In an age of brand labels and social media, this is a powerful filter. Before buying, ask whether you're paying for usefulness or for appearance. The difference often adds up to real savings and less stress.
cards.quote: Let us accustom ourselves to set aside mere outward show, and to measure things by their uses, not by their ornamental trappings
cards.apply_it: Before your next purchase, ask: 'Would I still buy this if nobody else ever saw it?'

quiz.question: How does Seneca say we should measure things?
options: By how much they impress others
By their uses, not their ornamental trappings
quiz.explanation: Seneca urges valuing things for their usefulness rather than for show.

cards.title: Read a few good books deeply rather than skimming many
cards.body:
Seneca criticises people who collect huge libraries they never read, using books as decoration for their dining rooms. A student, he says, is overwhelmed rather than taught by such a mass. It is better to devote yourself to a few authors than to wander through many.

The same applies to endless articles, feeds and saved links. Owning or bookmarking isn't learning. Pick a few excellent sources, go deep, and buy books to read, not to display.
cards.quote: A student is overwhelmed by such a mass, not instructed, and it is much better to devote yourself to a few writers than to skim through many.
cards.apply_it: Choose one book you've started but not finished. Commit to finishing it before buying or starting another.

quiz.question: What does Seneca say about huge collections of books?
options: They overwhelm rather than instruct; better to study a few writers
They are the mark of a true scholar
quiz.explanation: Seneca favours deep study of a few writers over skimming many or collecting for show.

cards.title: Even a hard situation has something good to be found in it
cards.body:
If you're trapped in a difficult situation you can't escape, Seneca advises, look for the compensations. People in chains suffer most at first; once they stop fretting and decide to bear it, they learn to carry the load more easily. Habit, he says, is nature's gift for softening misfortune.

A small room can be made liveable by clever arrangement, and good sense can ease what is harsh. This isn't pretending things are fine; it's refusing to let hardship blind you to whatever good is still within reach.
cards.quote: No condition can be so wretched that an impartial mind can find no compensations in it.
cards.apply_it: Think of a hard situation you can't change right now. Write down three things in it that are still good or useful.

quiz.question: According to Seneca, what helps people bear misfortune over time?
quiz.explanation: Habit softens hardship, and an impartial mind can find some good in any condition.

cards.title: Decide in advance where your success will stop
cards.body:
Seneca says nothing frees us from the swing between hope and fear so well as setting our own limit to success, rather than letting fortune decide when our run ends. Stop of your own accord, well before you seem to have to.

He also notes that people at the very top often can't climb down without falling. Setting a ceiling, such as a savings target, a business size, or a career level, lets ambition energise you without dragging you into vast, endless ventures.
cards.quote: Yet nothing sets as free from these alternations of hope and fear so well as always fixing some limit to our successes, and not allowing fortune to choose when to stop our career
cards.apply_it: For one goal you're chasing, write down the point at which you'd say 'that's enough'. Keep it somewhere visible.

quiz.question: What does Seneca say frees us from swinging between hope and fear?
options: Letting fortune decide when to stop
Setting our own limit to our successes
quiz.explanation: Choosing your own stopping point means fortune can't decide it for you.

cards.title: Hold what you have as if it were borrowed
cards.body:
Seneca describes the wise person as treating everything, from possessions and position to their body and life, as on loan. They look after it carefully, like a trustee managing someone else's property, and are ready to give it back gracefully when asked.

This isn't careless detachment. It's gratitude combined with realism: enjoy and care for what you have, without assuming it's permanently yours. When loss comes, as it eventually does, the thought 'it was lent to me' makes it easier to bear.
cards.quote: he lives as though he had borrowed them, and is ready to return them cheerfully whenever they are claimed.
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing you value (a possession, a role, a relationship). Spend a moment appreciating it as a loan you're lucky to have.

quiz.question: How does Seneca's wise man treat his possessions and even his body?
options: As worthless and not worth caring for
As borrowed, cared for and returned willingly
quiz.explanation: He treats all he has as on loan, caring for it but ready to give it back.

cards.title: What has happened to anyone can happen to you, so prepare now
cards.body:
Seneca quotes a playwright's line that whatever one person has suffered may happen to any of us. He lists the rich who became poor and the powerful who fell overnight. 'I never thought this would happen' is a cry of the unprepared.

His point isn't to live in dread. It's to build strength before trouble arrives: an emergency fund, a backup plan, a calm mental rehearsal. It's too late to train the mind for hardship once hardship is here. Expecting it takes away much of its power.
cards.quote: It is too late to school the mind to endurance of peril after peril has come.
cards.apply_it: Pick one risk you've been ignoring (job loss, illness, a broken phone). Take one concrete step to prepare for it this week.

quiz.question: Why does Seneca urge preparing for misfortune in advance?
options: It's too late to train the mind once trouble has come
Misfortune only happens to the unprepared
Preparation guarantees nothing bad will happen
quiz.explanation: Expecting what could happen removes much of adversity's power over us.

cards.title: Give every activity a purpose, or it's just restless idleness
cards.body:
Seneca describes people who rush around the city, in and out of houses and markets, looking busy. Ask where they're going and they say they don't know, but they'll see some people and do something. He compares them to ants crawling up and down a bush, gaining nothing, and calls it restless idleness.

Modern versions include endless scrolling, back-to-back meetings with no outcome, or busywork that just fills the day. Seneca's fix: give each action an aim, and know why you're doing it.
cards.quote: Let all your work, therefore, have some purpose, and keep some object in view
cards.apply_it: Before opening an app or starting a task today, finish the sentence: 'I'm doing this in order to…' If you can't, skip it.

quiz.question: What does Seneca compare purposeless busy people to?
options: Ants crawling up and down a bush
quiz.explanation: They move constantly without gaining anything, which Seneca calls restless idleness.

cards.title: Be flexible, but don't become fickle
cards.body:
Seneca recommends an easy-going temper: don't cling too tightly to your current situation, and be willing to move with whatever change comes. But he warns against caprice, constantly switching on a whim. Both extremes destroy peace: refusing to change anything, and being dissatisfied with everything.

The balance is to hold your plans lightly enough to adapt when life shifts, while having enough steadiness that you don't chase every new mood. Flexible, not fickle.
cards.quote: Both of these qualities, both that of altering nothing, and that of being dissatisfied with everything, are enemies to repose.
cards.apply_it: Think of a current plan. Is there one detail you're clinging to too tightly, or one you keep changing on a whim? Adjust it.

quiz.question: Which two extremes does Seneca say are enemies of peace?
options: Changing nothing and being dissatisfied with everything
quiz.explanation: Rigid stubbornness and restless caprice both disturb the mind's calm.

cards.title: Reframe a loss as lighter luggage
cards.body:
Seneca tells how Zeno, founder of the Stoic school, heard that a shipwreck had destroyed all his property. His reply: fortune wants him to pursue philosophy with less baggage. Instead of despairing, he turned the loss into a kind of freedom.

Not every loss can be reframed so easily, and grief is natural. But often, after the first shock, we can ask: what does this free me from? What can I now do differently? Seneca urges putting a good construction even on misfortunes.
cards.quote: Fortune bids me follow philosophy in lighter marching order.
cards.apply_it: Think of a past loss or setback. Write one way it made your life simpler or opened a new direction.

quiz.question: How did Zeno respond to losing all his property in a shipwreck?
options: He said fortune wanted him to travel lighter
quiz.explanation: Zeno reframed the loss as freedom to pursue philosophy with less baggage.

cards.title: Grieve honestly, not for show
cards.body:
Seneca observes that many people cry when others are watching and are dry-eyed once alone, because they think it shameful not to weep when everyone else does. We have become so guided by others' opinions, he says, that even grief, the simplest emotion, gets faked.

His advice is to give sorrow as much space as reason calls for, not as much as custom demands. Grief is real and deserves expression, but it should be your own, not a performance. Equally, nobody should judge how others grieve by outward signs.
cards.quote: So deeply has this evil of being guided by the opinion of others taken root in us, that even grief, the simplest of all emotions, begins to be counterfeited.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're expected to show a feeling, pause and ask what you actually feel. Express that honestly and respectfully.

quiz.question: What does Seneca say about grief shown for appearances?
options: People fake grief because they follow others' opinions
Grief should be hidden at all costs
Only the wise feel real grief
quiz.explanation: Concern for others' opinions has led people to counterfeit even grief.

cards.title: Alternate time alone with time among people
cards.body:
Seneca warns that mixing with people unlike us can unsettle our plans and stir passions we'd calmed. So we should retire into ourselves often. But he doesn't recommend permanent solitude either. Instead, alternate: time alone makes us long for company, and company makes us long for ourselves.

Each cures the other. If crowds and constant messages are wearing you down, take time alone. If you've been isolated and low, seek people out. The healthy rhythm moves between both.
cards.quote: solitude will cure us when we are sick of crowds, and crowds will cure us when we are sick of solitude.
cards.apply_it: Look at your week. If it's all people, schedule an hour alone. If it's mostly solitude, arrange to see a friend.

quiz.question: What does Seneca recommend about solitude and company?
options: Alternate between them so each cures the other
quiz.explanation: Solitude and society balance each other; each refreshes us when we tire of the other.

cards.title: Rest your mind like a field, or it will wear out
cards.body:
Seneca says the mind can't be kept at full stretch all the time. Like rich farmland that gets exhausted by nonstop harvests, a mind under unbroken work becomes dull and sluggish. A short rest restores its strength. He notes that Socrates played with children, and that the orator Asinius Pollio did no business after a set hour in the afternoon, not even reading letters.

Rest isn't laziness; it's maintenance. Walks outdoors, play, holidays and a firm end to the workday all help the mind come back stronger.
cards.quote: Men’s minds ought to have relaxation: they rise up better and more vigorous after rest.
cards.apply_it: Set a daily 'stop time' for work this week, after which you don't check work messages. Use the time for a walk or something playful.

quiz.question: Why does Seneca compare the mind to a rich field?
options: It must be worked harder each year
It produces more when never rested
Nonstop use exhausts it; rest restores it
It only needs attention once a year
quiz.explanation: Just as constant harvests exhaust soil, unbroken work dulls the mind; rest renews it.
